blocks.orig: If you have kids, you have surely looked at some picture books with African animals at some point. Wouldn’t it be amazing to see these animals in their natural habitat? Not only your little ones are dreaming about that, but probably also you, right? 😉 However, going to Tanzania on a safari with your kids might cause you some worries, and let us tell you: you are not alone! After all, you’ll be in a country far far away with wild animals roaming around close by, wherever you are.
blocks.html: Anyone with children has at some point leafed through a picture book full of African animals. How wonderful would it be to watch those very animals in the wild? It is not only your little ones who dream of that; chances are you do too, right? 😉 At the same time, the idea of a safari in Tanzania with your kids may give you a few worries, and believe us, you are not the only one. You will, after all, be in a country far, far away, with wild animals never far from wherever you happen to be.

blocks.orig: So it’s no surprise that we often get asked: “Is it even possible to go on a safari in Tanzania with kids?” We can tell you: yes, it is! And it’s much easier than you might think. In this article, our experienced travel consultant Julia Trento shares some insights, tips, and tricks for your family vacation in Tanzania. Spoiler alert: seeing the Big Five with your own eyes will leave you, your kids and even your teens in awe – and we all know how hard it can be to impress them.
blocks.html: No wonder, then, that one question comes up again and again: “Can you really go on safari in Tanzania with children?” Our answer is clear: yes, you can! And it is a lot simpler than you may imagine. In this article our experienced travel consultant Julia Trento shares her insights, tips and tricks for a family holiday in Tanzania. A small spoiler: seeing the Big Five with your own eyes will leave you, your kids and even your teenagers speechless – and we all know how difficult it is to impress them.

blocks.orig: There is no minimum age to enter Tanzanian national parks. And it gets better: as long as your kids are under the age of 15, you even pay a lower entry fee for them. Is it a sign? We think so! But let’s hear what Julia recommends.
blocks.html: Tanzanian national parks have no minimum age for entry. Better still: for children under 15 you pay a reduced entry fee. Could that be a sign? We think it is! But let’s hear what Julia suggests.

blocks.orig: “You as parents know your kids the best. When it comes to accommodation, we work with partners who are accustomed to kids. You need an extra bed for kids of any age? Simply book it on top. You want to enjoy one or two hours by yourself? Some lodges in Tanzania even offer childcare services with great programmes for the older kids!”
blocks.html: “Nobody knows your children better than you do as parents. For accommodation, we work with partners who are used to having kids around. Need an extra bed for a child of any age? Just add it to your booking. Fancy an hour or two to yourselves? Several lodges in Tanzania even provide childcare, with great programmes for the older children!”

blocks.orig: But just to give you an idea: most families who book a family-friendly safari with us have kids who are at least six years old. If you think that your kid is still a little too young for a safari, have a look at a holiday on Zanzibar, a paradisiac island just off the Tanzanian coast. Or you simply wait one, two, or three more years – Tanzania will be waiting for you.
blocks.html: To give you some perspective: in most families who book a family-friendly safari with us, the children are six or older. If you feel your child is still a bit too young for a safari, consider a holiday on Zanzibar, the paradise island just off the coast of Tanzania. Or simply wait another one, two or three years – Tanzania isn’t going anywhere.

blocks.orig: It’s all about the right preparation
blocks.html: It’s all down to good preparation

blocks.orig: Of course, there are a lot of things to organize when travelling with children.
blocks.html: Naturally, travelling with children means there is plenty to organise.

blocks.orig: “If you plan a family holiday in Tanzania with toddlers and your kids, best check with your doctor or health office regarding recommended vaccinations and medication. It’s also advisable to take out an additional Flying Doctors insurance. If something happens (knock on wood it won’t), a helicopter can transport you to the nearest hospital straight away.”
blocks.html: “When planning a family holiday in Tanzania with toddlers and older kids, it is best to ask your doctor or health office about recommended vaccinations and medication. Taking out additional Flying Doctors insurance is also a sensible idea. Should anything happen (touch wood it won’t), a helicopter can fly you straight to the nearest hospital.”

blocks.orig: On top of that, Julia has another good tip for travelling families: “Best book accommodation with a swimming pool so that the kids can have some fun after the game drives – and you as well.”
blocks.html: Julia has one more good tip for families on the road: “Choose accommodation with a swimming pool, so the children can let off steam after the game drives – and so can you.”

blocks.orig: And what about packing? It only needs a good system 😉 “Since you change accommodation several times, packing can become really annoying at some point. I recommend you already pick out the outfits at home and pack them into the suitcase as a set – underwear, socks, t-shirt, trousers, skirt, jumper, etc. If you stack all of these clothes on top of each other and then roll them up, you can save a lot of space. This way, you can simply take out the next outfit each morning, wrinkle-free! Put the dirty clothes in a separate bag, done!”
blocks.html: And packing? All it takes is a good system 😉 “Because you move between accommodations several times, packing can get really tedious after a while. My advice is to put the outfits together at home and pack each one into the suitcase as a set – underwear, socks, t-shirt, trousers, skirt, jumper and so on. Stack these clothes on top of one another and roll them up, and you save a surprising amount of space. Each morning you simply pull out the next outfit, crease-free! Dirty laundry goes into a separate bag, and that’s that!”

blocks.orig: 5 tips for the perfect child-friendly safari
blocks.html: Five tips for a perfect family-friendly safari

blocks.orig: No matter if the Serengeti or the Ngorongoro Conservation Area, Lake Manyara or Arusha National Park – it only takes a few little things to make your family safari unforgettable.
blocks.html: Whether you head for the Serengeti or the Ngorongoro Conservation Area, Lake Manyara or Arusha National Park, a few small details are all it takes to turn your family safari into something unforgettable.

blocks.orig: “We want to make sure that you can travel comfortably with your kids, for example with booster seats that can be rented for the cars. The safari jeeps are often also equipped with a fridge for milk etc. and if you let us know special dietary wishes of your little ones beforehand, we can accommodate them as well.”
blocks.html: “We want you to be able to travel in comfort with your children, which is why booster seats can be hired for the vehicles, for instance. The safari jeeps are often fitted with a fridge for milk and the like, and if you tell us about your little ones’ special dietary needs in advance, we can cater for those too.”

blocks.orig: On top of that, Julia has five more tips for a hassle-free safari for the whole family:
blocks.html: Julia also has five further tips for a stress-free safari with the whole family:

blocks.orig: 1. Bring some toys or order Wi-Fi in the car in case your kids get a little bored.
blocks.html: 1. Pack a few toys, or ask for Wi-Fi in the vehicle, in case the children get a bit restless.

blocks.orig: 2. Bring snacks and drinks, or order special snacks and drinks with us, so that no one of you gets hangry during the adventure.
blocks.html: 2. Take snacks and drinks along, or order special snacks and drinks through us, so nobody in the family gets hangry on the adventure.

blocks.orig: 4. Diaper bags are handy if you have to change nappies but don’t have a bin somewhere close.
blocks.html: 4. A nappy bag comes in useful when you need to change a nappy and there is no bin nearby.

blocks.orig: 5. Don’t forget sunscreen and insect repellant – that’s always important, no matter if you travel with or without kids 😉
blocks.html: 5. Remember the sunscreen and insect repellent – that matters whether you travel with children or without 😉

blocks.orig: Willemijn de Vrieze went on a safari with her two kids, Michiel and Jeroen (four and two years old).
blocks.html: Willemijn de Vrieze took her two sons, Michiel and Jeroen (aged four and two), on safari.

blocks.orig: “What I really like about the Tanzanian culture is that everyone is so kind to the kids and takes care of them. Everybody speaks to them, help at the pool or in the restaurant and sings with them. It’s always fun and never gets boring. And everyone knows that travelling with kids can be a challenge, so everyone is extremely helpful.
blocks.html: “What I love about Tanzanian culture is how kind everyone is to children and how they look after them. People talk to them, lend a hand at the pool or in the restaurant and sing with them. It is always fun and never dull. And because everyone understands that travelling with kids can be a challenge, everyone is incredibly helpful.

blocks.orig: Michiel and Jeroen had so much fun spotting and identifying the animals in the wild and were so proud when they saw another one. Rama, our guide, stopped immediately when he saw a fascinating animal. At some point Michiel even said: okay thanks, Rama, we can go on now!”.
blocks.html: Michiel and Jeroen had a wonderful time spotting and naming the animals in the wild, and were so proud every time they found another one. Our guide Rama pulled over straight away whenever he saw something fascinating. At one point Michiel actually said: okay thanks, Rama, we can carry on now!”.

blocks.orig: And what about older kids and teenagers?
blocks.html: What about older children and teenagers?

blocks.orig: Everything up to this point also applies for travelling to Africa with older kids or teenagers (except the diaper bag). Of course, you can, and should, go on a safari with them as well, but there are also many other activities they will surely like. These are our top three:
blocks.html: All of the above applies just as much to travelling to Africa with older kids or teenagers (apart from the nappy bag). You can, and should, take them on safari too, but there are plenty of other activities they are bound to enjoy. Here are our top three:

blocks.orig: These natural hot springs between Arusha and Moshi are the perfect spot for your kids. They can jump into the crystal blue water with a rope, relax in a tube and take countless pictures in, under and at the water. Instagrammable? 100%!
blocks.html: These natural hot springs between Arusha and Moshi are an ideal spot for kids. They can swing into the crystal-blue water on a rope, drift around in a tube and take endless photos in, under and beside the water. Instagrammable? Absolutely!

blocks.orig: If a typical safari is “too boring” for your teens, they can also join an experienced guide on a walking safari, diving even deeper into nature and getting even closer to the wild animals. Now there’s something they can tell their friends after the holidays.
blocks.html: Should a regular safari be “too boring” for your teenagers, they can head out with an experienced guide on a walking safari instead, going deeper into nature and getting even closer to the wild animals. That gives them a story to tell their friends once the holidays are over.

blocks.orig: If your kids are somewhat older, and you want to include a trip to Zanzibar in your family holiday, head up north during a full moon and let them go to the Kendwa Full Moon Party… with you of course – they’re going to love you (even more!).
blocks.html: With slightly older children, and a stay on Zanzibar as part of your family holiday, travel to the north of the island at full moon and let them go to the Kendwa Full Moon Party… accompanied by you, naturally – they will love you (even more!).

blocks.orig: Joshua Mbaga, one of our German- and English-speaking guides, says: “I really love taking families on a safari since I get along super well with kids. And the feeling is mutual: I have been working for Your Tanzania Trip for four years and have received only good reviews from the little ones, my biggest critics. I think it’s really cool and fun to tell kids gripping stories about nature, the Big Five and of course lion cubs, just as in the Lion King.”
blocks.html: Joshua Mbaga, one of our guides who speaks German and English, puts it like this: “I really enjoy taking families on safari because I get on brilliantly with kids. And the feeling is mutual: in my four years working for Your Tanzania Trip I have had nothing but good reviews from the little ones, my toughest critics. I find it really cool and fun to tell children gripping stories about nature, the Big Five and of course lion cubs, just like in the Lion King.”

blocks.orig: Our German-speaking guide, Timothy Kinango Msuya, agrees: “Kids are little angels. I also have kids myself, and to me, it’s a lot of fun going on safaris with my youngest guests. Even if there are some challenges here and there – we all know what it can be like. I love them, and travelling with families is the favourite part of my job. I don’t see any difficulty going on a safari with kids, quite the contrary: it’s a blessing for me having the opportunity to show them my country.”
blocks.html: Timothy Kinango Msuya, our German-speaking guide, feels the same: “Children are little angels. I have kids of my own, and for me going on safari with my youngest guests is great fun. Sure, there are challenges now and then – we all know how that goes. But I love them, and travelling with families is the part of my job I enjoy most. I don’t see any problem with taking children on safari, quite the opposite: being able to show them my country is a blessing.”
